mainTopic: How הצד השוה works (including רבינא's falling wall), the word חב, and the dispute over paying damages from 'the best land'
overview: This amud first finishes the discussion of what the words הַצַּד הַשָּׁוֶה in the opening משנה come to add. Through a back-and-forth between שור and בור, the גמרא shows that each one answers the other's weakness, so a case can be learned from what they share. רבינא then applies the same method to a wall or tree that falls into the street after בית דין told the owner to take it down. Next the גמרא explains why the משנה uses the short word חב instead of חייב: the תנא was from ירושלים and spoke briefly. It then brings a ברייתא where רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא argue about whose 'best land' the פסוק means when a damager pays. After one explanation is rejected by רבא, רב אחא בר יעקב explains that they argue about whether land quality is measured by the damaged person's land or the damager's, and the גמרא shows how each reads the פסוק. Finally the גמרא asks what רבי עקיבא's קל וחומר for הקדש refers to. It settles on a vow to give money to the בית המקדש and begins to challenge that answer, a challenge that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The ox category proves the point
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the objection raised just before by pointing to שור: an ox is in the public domain with permission, and its owner still pays.
steps.simpleTranslation: Ox will prove it!
steps.whatsHappening: Just before this, someone objected that you cannot learn this case from בור. Now the גמרא answers by saying the category of שור shows that the objection does not matter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The objection was about a feature that בור has and our case lacks. An ox lacks that same feature, since it walks in the public domain with permission, yet its owner is חייב. So that feature cannot be the reason for liability.

keyTerms.meaning: Will prove. Used when one case shows that a suggested difference does not matter.
Ox. One of the main categories of damage (אבות נזיקין).

steps.confusionAlert: This line answers an objection from the previous discussion, so it may feel like it starts in the middle. It does. The גמרא is defending a derivation it began before this point.

phrases.english: Ox will prove it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection to learning from בור that was raised just before this section
steps.terutzResolutionType: Counter-example from another category (פירכא answered with יוכיח)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The case could only be learned from בור, and בור has a special feature that our case lacks.
steps.terutzMaskana: שור lacks that feature and is still liable, so the feature is not what creates liability.

steps.title: But an ox normally goes and does damage
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: שור is different, because it is the nature of an ox to move around and cause damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: What about an ox? An ox is different, because its way is to go around and cause damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the proof from שור. It points out a feature the ox has that our case does not have.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ox moves and damages on its own, which is a strong reason to hold its owner responsible. Our case has nothing that moves around and causes damage. So maybe we cannot learn from שור after all.

keyTerms.meaning: What about...? It is different, because... The standard way to point out a weakness in a comparison.
Its normal way is to move around and cause damage.

phrases.english: What about an ox?
It is different, because its way is to go and do damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the proof from שור given in step 1
steps.kashyaTarget: The use of שור as a source for liability in our case
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שור has its own special feature (it moves and damages), which our case lacks. So the comparison breaks down.

steps.title: The pit category proves the point
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: בור does not move around and cause damage, yet its owner is still liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: Pit will prove it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge against שור by pointing back to בור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A pit just sits there and does not go anywhere, yet its owner pays. So "moving around and doing damage" is not needed for liability. Each category fills in what the other is missing.

keyTerms.meaning: Pit. A main category of damage where an obstacle is left in a public place.
Will prove. Will prove it (same meaning as יוֹכִיחַ).

phrases.english: Pit will prove it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 2
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only something that moves and damages, like an ox, makes its owner liable.
steps.terutzMaskana: בור does not move and still makes its owner liable, so moving is not required.

steps.title: The reasoning comes back around to the common feature
steps.stepSummary: Since each category answers the weakness of the other, the law is learned from what שור and בור have in common. That is what הצד השוה adds.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the reasoning has come back around.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wraps up: we learn the case from the shared feature of both categories together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Neither שור alone nor בור alone works, because each has a special feature someone can point to. But each one shows that the other's special feature is not the real reason. So the liability comes from what they share. This is the case that the word הצד השוה in the משנה comes to include.

keyTerms.meaning: The reasoning has come back around. We return to learning from the common feature of both sources.
The common feature. A method of learning a law from what two sources share.

steps.whatToRemember: When two sources each have a weakness, but each one cancels the other's weakness, we learn the law from what they share. This is called הצד השוה. That is how the case discussed before this section is included by the משנה.

phrases.english: And the reasoning has come back around.
phrases.notes: In other words, we are back to learning from both sources together, from what they have in common.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the back-and-forth of steps 1 through 3
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The case is learned through הצד השוה of שור and בור. This explains why the משנה mentions הצד השוה.

steps.title: רבינא: the common feature includes a falling wall or tree
steps.stepSummary: רבינא gives a different case that הצד השוה comes to include. A wall or tree falls into the public domain and causes damage after בית דין gave its owner a deadline to remove it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: it comes to include what we learned in a משנה. If a wall or a tree fell into the public domain and caused damage, the owner does not have to pay. If they gave him time to cut down the tree or knock down the wall, and they fell within that time and caused damage, he does not pay. If they fell after that time, he must pay.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא offers a different answer to "what does הצד השוה add?" He points to a case from another משנה: a wall or tree that falls after the owner was told to remove it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the owner of a wall or tree that suddenly falls is פטור, because it was not his fault. Once בית דין has given him a deadline and it passes, he is חייב. According to רבינא, that liability is not learned from any single category alone. It is the case that הצד השוה in our משנה comes to include.

keyTerms.meaning: To include. To bring in an additional case.
That which we learned in a משנה.
The public domain.
Exempt from paying / obligated to pay.
A set period of time, here a deadline given to the owner.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two time periods. Inside the deadline, the owner is still פטור. Only after the deadline passes does he become חייב.
steps.whyThisMatters: This opens a second explanation of what הצד השוה includes. It also teaches a practical rule: once an owner has been warned to fix a danger and does not, he is responsible for the damage.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
It comes to include this that we learned in a mishna:
phrases.notes: "It" is the phrase "the common feature" (הצד השוה) in our משנה.

phrases.english: A wall or a tree
that fell into the public domain
and caused damage: he is exempt from paying.
If they gave him time
phrases.notes: "They" means בית דין, who saw the danger and set him a deadline.

phrases.english: to cut down the tree
and to knock down the wall,
and they fell within the time
and caused damage: he is exempt.
After the time: he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different case that הצד השוה includes, instead of the case worked out in steps 1 through 4
steps.mimraCoreRuling: הצד השוה in the משנה includes liability for a wall or tree that falls into the public domain and causes damage after the deadline set by בית דין has passed. Within the deadline, the owner is exempt.

steps.title: If the owner gave it up, isn't the fallen wall just a pit?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the exact case is. If the owner gave up ownership of the fallen wall or tree, then both רב and שמואל would agree it is simply a type of בור, so הצד השוה is not needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: What exactly is the case? If he gave up ownership of it, then according to both רב and שמואל it is the same as a pit. What is special about a pit? Its damage is common, and you are responsible to guard it. These too: their damage is common, and you are responsible to guard them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבינא. It argues that a fallen wall or tree, once the owner gives it up, is really just a בור. Then there is no need for הצד השוה to teach it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two key features of a בור are that its damage is common and that guarding it is your job. A fallen wall or tree that the owner gave up has both features. So it fits under בור by itself, and רבינא's case adds nothing new.

keyTerms.meaning: What are the exact circumstances?
He gave up ownership of it (made it ownerless)
That is the same as בור
Its damage is common, likely to happen
Guarding it is your responsibility

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
If he declared it ownerless,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין לְרַב בֵּין לִשְׁמוּאֵל – הַיְינוּ בּוֹר;
phrases.english: according to both Rav and Shmuel, this is Pit;
phrases.notes: רב and שמואל disagree about obstacles in the street. Once the owner has given the thing up, though, both agree it counts as a בור.

phrases.english: what is special about Pit?
That its damage is common,
and guarding it is upon you;
these too:
their damage is common,
and guarding them is upon you!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבינא's case from Step 5 by claiming it is already covered by בור.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבינא's claim that הצד השוה is needed for the falling wall or tree
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A wall or tree that the owner gave up has the same defining features as בור, common damage and a duty to guard, so it is simply a type of בור.

steps.title: If the owner kept it, it is still a pit according to שמואל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא covers the other possibility. Even if the owner did not give up the wall or tree, שמואל learns all street obstacles from בור. So it would still be a type of בור.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he did not give them up, then according to שמואל, who says 'We learned all of them from his pit,' it is the same as a pit!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its challenge by covering the second option, where the owner did not give the wall or tree up. Either way, the case seems to fall under בור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל holds that any obstacle a person puts in the street is learned from בור, whether or not he gave it up. So the 'not given up' option also lands back at בור, at least according to שמואל. Both possible cases now seem to make הצד השוה unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: He did not give up ownership of them
We learned all of them (street obstacles) from his pit

phrases.english: If he did not declare them ownerless,
according to Shmuel, who says:
We learned all of them from his pit,
phrases.notes: "All of them" means every obstacle a person leaves in the street, whether or not he gave it up.

phrases.english: this is Pit!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the two-sided challenge begun in Step 6 by covering the case where the owner did not give the item up.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבינא's case, in the scenario where the owner kept ownership
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: According to שמואל, all street obstacles are learned from בור even without giving them up, so this option also reduces to בור.

steps.title: A wall or tree is not like a pit, because it was not made to cause damage
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the case really is one where the owner gave the item up. Even so, it is not the same as בור. A pit is damaging from the moment it is dug, while a wall or tree was not made in a damaging way.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, the case is where he gave them up, and they are not like a pit. What about a pit? From the very start it is made in a way that causes damage. Can you say the same about these, which from the start are not made in a way that causes damage?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבינא. It shows a real difference between a בור and a fallen wall or tree, so you cannot learn the wall from בור alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Digging a pit creates a hazard right away. Building a wall or planting a tree is normal and harmless, and the danger came only later when it fell. Because of this weakness, בור alone cannot teach the wall's law, and something more like הצד השוה is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: Really / actually (keeps the first option after all)
And it is not similar
What about...? (pointing out a special feature that blocks a comparison)
From the start it was made in a damaging way

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying a fallen wall has nothing to do with בור. It only says that בור alone is not enough to teach it, because of one difference.

phrases.english: Actually, it is where he declared them ownerless;
and they are not similar to Pit:
what about Pit?
That from its very start it is made for damage;
will you say so about these,
which from their very start are not made for damage?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Steps 6-7 by distinguishing the wall or tree from בור.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction (חילוק): a feature found in בור is missing from the new case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A fallen wall or tree that the owner gave up is simply a בור, so הצד השוה adds nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: A בור is damaging from the start, and a wall or tree is not, so בור alone cannot teach this case.

steps.title: The ox proves that 'not made for damage' does not exempt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points to שור. An ox is not created to cause damage, yet its owner pays. So the difference just raised does not exempt the owner of the wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ox will prove it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the difference from Step 8 by pointing to שור. This sets up the next move, where the law will be built from what בור and שור share.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 said a wall is unlike a בור because it was not made to damage. An ox also was not born to damage, yet its owner is liable. So 'not made for damage' cannot be a reason to exempt the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: Will prove (a case that shows a proposed difference does not matter)

steps.whyThisMatters: Bringing in שור against the weakness of בור is the first half of a הצד השוה argument, just like the pattern in Steps 1-4.

phrases.english: Ox will prove it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the distinction from בור made in Step 8 by pointing to שור.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 8 that 'not made for damage' sets the wall apart
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שור was not made for damage either, yet its owner pays, so that feature cannot exempt the wall's owner.

steps.title: An ox goes out and damages, but a wall does not
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on learning the wall or tree from שור. An ox moves around and damages by its nature, and a wall or tree does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: What about an ox? An ox's way is to walk around and cause damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now finds a weak point in learning from שור. A wall or tree does not move and damage the way an ox does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 9 the גמרא used שור to answer the difference that came from בור. Now שור has a special feature of its own: it walks around and causes damage. Since a wall or tree does not do this, it seems we cannot learn from שור either.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What about...?' A standard way to say a source has a special feature, so we cannot learn from it.
Its way is to go and cause damage. It moves around and damages by its nature.
A pushback that shows one source is different, so it cannot be used as a proof.

phrases.english: What about an ox?
Its way is to go and cause damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Step 9 used שור to answer the point taken from בור. Now שור itself is shown to have a special feature.
steps.kashyaTarget: Using שור as a source for the owner of a fallen wall or tree having to pay.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An ox moves and damages by its nature. A wall or tree does not, so a wall or tree cannot be learned from שור.

steps.title: Pit proves the point, and we go back to what they share
steps.stepSummary: בור shows that 'going out to damage' is not needed for an owner to pay. So the proof goes back to the shared feature of בור and שור.
steps.simpleTranslation: A pit proves it! A pit does not walk around, and its owner still pays. So we go back to the shared reasoning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 10 by pointing to בור, which does not move and still makes its owner pay. Then it says the proof returns to the shared feature of בור and שור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each source answers the weak point of the other. בור shows that moving around is not needed, and שור (step 9) shows that being made to damage is not needed. So the two together teach the wall or tree through what they share. That is the הצד השוה רבינא described in step 5.

keyTerms.meaning: Will prove. One case is brought to show that a feature does not decide the law.
And the reasoning goes back to its start. We return to learning from what the sources share.
The shared feature. A law learned from what two sources have in common.

steps.whatToRemember: A fallen wall or tree that the owner was told to remove is learned from the shared feature of בור and שור. Each source's special feature is answered by the other, so the owner pays.

phrases.english: A pit will prove it!
And the reasoning goes back to the start.
phrases.notes: We go back to learning from what בור and שור have in common.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 10 by showing that the special feature of שור does not decide the law, and closes the הצד השוה discussion.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Each source cancels the other's special feature (תוכיח, then חזר הדין).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might think the wall cannot be learned from שור, because an ox moves around and damages.
steps.terutzMaskana: בור shows that moving is not what makes an owner pay. The shared feature of בור and שור teaches that the owner of the wall or tree pays.

steps.title: Why does the משנה say חב instead of חייב?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's words 'חב המזיק' and asks why it did not use the usual word, חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: when it damages, the damager is חב. Why חב? It should have said חייב!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to a new line of the משנה and asks about an unusual word in it. This step sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The normal word in the משנה for 'obligated' is חייב. Here the משנה says חב, which is unusual. The question is only about the wording, not about the law.

keyTerms.meaning: Obligated. A short, unusual form of the word.
Obligated or liable. The usual word in the משנה.
It should have said.
The one who causes the damage, or the owner of what caused it.

phrases.english: When it damages, the damager is obligated (חב).
'The damager is חב'?!
It should have said 'the damager is חייב'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The הצד השוה discussion is finished. The גמרא now turns to the next phrase of the משנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The usual word is חייב, so the unusual word חב needs an explanation.

steps.title: The תנא was from ירושלים and spoke briefly
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה says in the name of רב that this תנא was from ירושלים, where people used short wording. That is why he said חב.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: this תנא is from ירושלים, and he teaches in short, light language.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the wording question. The word חב is simply this תנא's short way of speaking.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing in the law changes, because חב means the same as חייב. The different word comes from the speaking style of the תנא who taught this משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: A teacher from the time of the משנה.
From ירושלים.
Light language. Short, quick wording.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
This תנא is from Jerusalem,
who teaches in light (short) language.
phrases.notes: חב is a shorter word than חייב.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: הַאי תַּנָּא יְרוּשַׁלְמִי הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording question of step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the word by the style of the תנא who said it.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might think חב was chosen to teach something special.
steps.terutzMaskana: חב means חייב. It is just the short style of a תנא from ירושלים.

steps.title: Whose best land? רבי ישמעאל says the victim's
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's words about paying for damage. It brings a ברייתא where רבי ישמעאל says the פסוק's 'best of his field' means the best field of the person who was damaged.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'to pay payments of damage.' The Rabbis taught: the פסוק says 'from the best of his field and the best of his vineyard he shall pay.' This means the best field and best vineyard of the person who was damaged. These are the words of רבי ישמעאל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic: what quality of land the damager must pay with. It brings רבי ישמעאל's opinion from a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says 'his field' and 'his vineyard' but does not say whose. רבי ישמעאל says 'his' means the one who was damaged. So the payment is measured by the victim's best land.

keyTerms.meaning: The best. The top quality of land.
The one who was damaged.
His field.
His vineyard.

steps.confusionAlert: 'His field' in the פסוק could sound like the damager's field. רבי ישמעאל reads it as the field of the one who was damaged.

phrases.english: To pay the payments of damage.
The Rabbis taught:
'The best of his field and the best of his vineyard he shall pay':
the best field of the one who was damaged,
and the best vineyard of the one who was damaged.
These are the words of Rabbi Yishmael.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״מֵיטַב שָׂדֵהוּ וּמֵיטַב כַּרְמוֹ יְשַׁלֵּם״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The wording question is finished. The גמרא moves to the next phrase of the משנה, about payment.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי ישמעאל: 'his field' and 'his vineyard' in the פסוק mean those of the one who was damaged. The payment is measured by the victim's best land.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: the damaged person collects from the best land
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא says the פסוק 'מיטב שדהו' teaches that נזקין are collected from עידית, the best-quality land. With a קל וחומר, the same is true for הקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא says: The verse only comes to let damaged people collect from the best-quality land. And all the more so, the Temple treasury collects from the best land.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא from step 14 continues. Now רבי עקיבא gives a different reading of the same פסוק that רבי ישמעאל explained.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ישמעאל read 'the best of his field' as the best field of the person who was damaged. רבי עקיבא reads it as a rule about collecting: payment for damages comes from the damager's best land. He then adds that הקדש gets at least this much, through a קל וחומר.

keyTerms.meaning: Best-quality land
People who were damaged, or the laws of damages
An 'all the more so' argument
Property that belongs to the בית המקדש

steps.confusionAlert: רבי עקיבא is not saying the damager pays more than the damage. He is only saying which land the payment is taken from: the best land.

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says:
The verse comes only
to let damaged people collect from the best-quality land.
phrases.notes: He means the damager's best land, unlike רבי ישמעאל, who spoke about the damaged person's field.

phrases.english: And all the more so for consecrated property.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר: לֹא בָּא הַכָּתוּב אֶלָּא לִגְבּוֹת לַנִּזָּקִין מִן הָעִידִּית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is the second opinion in the same ברייתא, giving a different reading of 'מיטב שדהו' from רבי ישמעאל's.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Damages are collected from the damager's best land (עידית), and הקדש collects from it all the more so.

steps.title: How can he pay for a rich bed if his animal ate a poor one?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי ישמעאל. His view seems to mean that even if the animal ate a poor garden bed, the owner pays the value of a rich one. That would be paying more than the damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to רבי ישמעאל: if the animal ate from a rich bed, he pays for a rich one. But if it ate from a poor bed, does he still pay for a rich one?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to רבי ישמעאל and questions how his view could make sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ישמעאל said payment is measured by the damaged person's best field. Taken plainly, that means a person whose animal ate a poor bed still pays as if it ate a rich one. The גמרא finds that hard to accept, because he would be paying more than what was destroyed.

keyTerms.meaning: Rich, high-quality (garden bed or field)
Poor, low-quality (garden bed or field)

phrases.english: And according to Rabbi Yishmael,
if it ate a rich one, he pays for a rich one;
phrases.notes: 'It' is the animal, and 'one' is a garden bed. The גמרא leaves these words out but assumes them.

phrases.english: if it ate a poor one, does he pay for a rich one?!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל, אָכַל שְׁמֵינָה – מְשַׁלֵּם שְׁמֵינָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After quoting רבי עקיבא, the גמרא returns to challenge the opinion of רבי ישמעאל from step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ישמעאל's rule that payment is measured by the damaged person's best field
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A damager should pay for what was destroyed, not more. Paying for a rich bed when a poor one was eaten seems unfair.

steps.title: רב אידי בר אבין: we don't know which bed was eaten
steps.stepSummary: רב אידי בר אבין explains that רבי ישמעאל is talking about an animal that ate one garden bed among many, when we do not know if it was a poor one or a rich one. In that case the owner pays for a rich one.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rav Idi bar Avin said: What case are we dealing with here? A case where the animal ate a garden bed among other garden beds, and we don't know whether it ate a poor one or a rich one. In that case he pays for a rich one.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אידי בר אבין answers the question by narrowing the case. רבי ישמעאל does not mean the animal surely ate a poor bed. He means we are not sure which bed it ate.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem was paying for a rich bed when a poor bed was clearly eaten. רב אידי בר אבין moves the case to one of doubt. When we cannot tell which bed was eaten, רבי ישמעאל says the owner pays the higher value.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (a way of narrowing the case)
A garden bed, a small planted plot
We do not know

phrases.english: Rav Idi bar Avin said:
Here, what are we dealing with?
For example, where it ate a garden bed among the garden beds,
and we don't know whether it ate a poor one
or it ate a rich one;
in that case he pays for a rich one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 16 by limiting רבי ישמעאל's rule to a case of doubt.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי ישמעאל seemed to say the damager pays for a rich bed even when he surely damaged a poor one.
steps.terutzMaskana: He is speaking only about a case where we don't know which bed was eaten. Then the owner pays for a rich one.

steps.title: רבא: the one who wants money must bring proof
steps.stepSummary: רבא attacks רב אידי בר אבין's answer. If the owner pays only for a poor bed when we know the animal ate a poor one, how can he pay more when we are unsure? The rule is that the one who takes money from another must bring the proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: If we knew it ate a poor bed, he would pay only for a poor one. Now that we don't know whether it ate a poor one or a rich one, should he pay for a rich one?! The one who takes money from his fellow has to bring the proof!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא challenges the answer of רב אידי בר אבין from step 17 and shows it goes against a basic rule of monetary law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא uses a 'how much more so' style of argument. Being unsure cannot make the damager pay more than being sure that the bed was poor. Because of the rule המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה, the damaged person must prove the bed was rich, or he gets only the lower value.

keyTerms.meaning: The one who wants to take money from another must bring proof
Now, in this case

steps.whyThisMatters: המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה is a basic rule in all money cases. In a doubt, money stays with whoever is holding it unless the other side brings proof.

phrases.english: Rava said:
Now, if we knew that it ate a poor one,
he would pay only for a poor one;
now that we don't know

phrases.aramaic: אִי כְּחוּשָׁה אֲכַל אִי שְׁמֵינָה אֲכַל,
phrases.english: whether it ate a poor one or ate a rich one,
should he pay for a rich one?!
The one who takes money from his fellow must bring the proof!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: וּמָה אִילּוּ יָדְעִינַן דִּכְחוּשָׁה אֲכַל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the explanation of רבי ישמעאל that רב אידי בר אבין gave in step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אידי בר אבין's claim that in a case of doubt the damager pays for a rich bed
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Doubt cannot make him pay more than certainty about a poor bed would. Also, the damaged person is the one trying to take money, so he must prove the bed was rich (המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה).

steps.title: A new case: the damaged person's best land equals the damager's worst land
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר יעקב rejects the earlier answer. He explains that the dispute is about a case where the ניזק's עידית is the same quality as the מזיק's זיבורית.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב אחא בר יעקב said: What case are we dealing with here? A case where the best land of the damaged person is like the worst land of the one who did the damage.
steps.whatsHappening: Since רבא pushed away רב אידי בר אבין's answer, the גמרא brings a brand-new way to understand רבי ישמעאל. It changes the case so that nobody pays more than the damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem in Step 16 was that רבי ישמעאל seemed to make the damager overpay. רב אחא בר יעקב says the argument is not about how much to pay. It is about which piece of land counts as 'the best' when payment is made with land. The damaged person's top land is only as good as the damager's poorest land, so 'best' means two different things depending on whose land we look at.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (the גמרא is narrowing the case)
Best-quality land
Poorest-quality land
The one who was damaged
The one who caused the damage

steps.confusionAlert: This is not saying anyone pays more money than the damage was worth. The amount stays the same. The question is only which quality of land is handed over as payment.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר יַעֲקֹב:
phrases.english: Rather, Rav Acha bar Yaakov said:
With what are we dealing here?
For example, where the best land of the injured party
was like the worst land of the one who caused damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר יַעֲקֹב: הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רב אידי בר אבין's answer (Step 17), which רבא rejected in Step 18.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי ישמעאל seemed to make the damager pay the value of a rich bed even for eating a poor one, or to pay extra when we are unsure.
steps.terutzMaskana: The amount paid always matches the damage. The dispute is only about which quality of land counts as 'best' when the land qualities of the two people do not match.

steps.title: The dispute: whose land do we measure by?
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל measures 'best' by the ניזק's land, and רבי עקיבא measures it by the מזיק's land.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what they argue about: רבי ישמעאל holds we measure by the damaged person's land, and רבי עקיבא holds we measure by the damager's land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now spells out exactly what the two תנאים disagree about in the case just described.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי ישמעאל, the standard is the damaged person's best land. The damager's poor land is as good as that, so he may pay with it. For רבי עקיבא, the standard is the damager's own best land, so he must pay with his עידית.

keyTerms.meaning: And in this they argue
We assess / measure the value

steps.whatToRemember: רבי ישמעאל measures by the damaged person's land, so the damager can pay with poorer land. רבי עקיבא measures by the damager's land, so he pays with his own best.

phrases.english: And in this they disagree:
Rabbi Yishmael holds: we assess by the land of the injured party,
and Rabbi Akiva holds: we assess by the land of the one who caused damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רב אחא בר יעקב's answer by stating the exact point of the dispute.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי ישמעאל: the quality of land is measured by the ניזק's land. רבי עקיבא: it is measured by the מזיק's land.

steps.title: What is רבי ישמעאל's source?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what reason רבי ישמעאל has for measuring by the damaged person's land.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is רבי ישמעאל's reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the source of רבי ישמעאל's view. This line sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now that the dispute is clear, the גמרא wants to see how each side reads the פסוק. It starts with רבי ישמעאל, because his reading needs a source: the plain words 'his field' sound like the field of the one who pays, not the damaged person's.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?

phrases.english: What is the reason of Rabbi Yishmael?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source behind רבי ישמעאל's side of the dispute stated in Step 20.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which פסוק or reading leads רבי ישמעאל to measure by the ניזק's land.

steps.title: The word 'field' at the top and bottom of the פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The word 'שדה' appears twice in the פסוק. The top one is the damaged person's field, so the bottom one is too.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Field' is said below, and 'field' is said above. Just as the field said above belongs to the damaged person, so too the field said below belongs to the damaged person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי ישמעאל learns from the same word 'field' appearing twice in one פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The beginning of the פסוק says the animal ate 'in the field of another', which is clearly the damaged person's field. רבי ישמעאל says the second 'field' in 'מיטב שדהו' should mean the same thing. So 'best' is measured by the damaged person's field.

keyTerms.meaning: Below (later in the פסוק)
Above (earlier in the פסוק)
Field

phrases.english: "Field" is stated below,
phrases.notes: שמות 22:4. 'Below' is the end of the פסוק: 'the best of his field'.

phrases.english: and "field" is stated above;
phrases.notes: 'Above' is earlier in the same פסוק, where the animal eats 'in the field of another'.

phrases.english: just as the field stated above is of the injured party,
so too the field stated below is of the injured party.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A comparison of the two places 'שדה' appears in the פסוק: the first is the ניזק's field, so the second is too.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: 'his field' means the payer's field
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא reads 'מיטב שדהו' simply. 'His' refers to the one who pays, so the standard is the מזיק's best land.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי עקיבא says: 'The best of his field and the best of his vineyard he shall pay' means the best of the one who is paying.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives רבי עקיבא's reading of the same פסוק, which explains why he measures by the damager's land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'he shall pay' are right next to 'his field', so רבי עקיבא connects them: it is the field of the one paying. That is why the damager must pay from his own עידית. This plain reading raises a question for רבי ישמעאל, which the next step answers.

keyTerms.meaning: The best
His vineyard
He shall pay
Of that one who is paying

steps.whatToRemember: Both תנאים agree payment is from 'the best'. רבי ישמעאל reads 'his field' as the damaged person's field, by comparing it to 'field' earlier in the פסוק. רבי עקיבא reads it as the field of the one who pays.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Akiva:
"The best of his field and the best of his vineyard he shall pay"
means of that one who is paying.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, ״מֵיטַב שָׂדֵהוּ וּמֵיטַב כַּרְמוֹ יְשַׁלֵּם״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רבי עקיבא's reading, after רבי ישמעאל's reading in Step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי עקיבא connects 'his field' to 'he shall pay', so the field is the payer's. This means the מזיק must give his own best land.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל keeps both the comparison and the plain verse
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל answers that the גזרה שוה and the simple meaning of the פסוק each teach something.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how does רבי ישמעאל deal with the simple reading? The word comparison does its job, and the verse itself also does its job. The comparison does its job the way I already explained.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how רבי ישמעאל responds to רבי עקיבא's simple reading of 'שדהו'. He answers that both the גזרה שוה and the plain פסוק each teach a lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא read 'his field' as the מזיק's field, which seems to clash with רבי ישמעאל's גזרה שוה. רבי ישמעאל says nothing has to be thrown out. The גזרה שוה stays as already explained: the standard is the ניזק's best land. The next step shows what the plain פסוק adds.

keyTerms.meaning: It works, it is useful for teaching something
A teaching drawn from the same word appearing in two places
The verse, read simply
As I said before

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yishmael [how does he respond]?
The verbal comparison is effective,
and the verse [itself] is effective;
the verbal comparison is effective, as I said.
phrases.notes: This points back to step 22: the second 'שדה' is the ניזק's field, so we measure 'best' by his land.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל – אַהֲנִי גְּזֵרָה שָׁוָה, וְאַהְנִי קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the hidden challenge from רבי עקיבא's simple reading in step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Both readings are kept, each teaching a different lesson
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי ישמעאל's גזרה שוה seems to cancel the simple meaning of 'שדהו', the מזיק's field.
steps.terutzMaskana: The גזרה שוה sets the standard by the ניזק's land, and the plain פסוק still teaches its own lesson.

steps.title: The case the plain verse teaches according to רבי ישמעאל
steps.stepSummary: The plain words 'מיטב שדהו' teach that when the מזיק's worst land is below the ניזק's best, the מזיק must pay from his own best land.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse does its job in this case. The מזיק has good land and poor land, and the ניזק has good land. The מזיק's poor land is not as good as the ניזק's good land. Here the מזיק pays from his own best land. He cannot say, 'Come collect from my poor land.' Instead, the ניזק collects from the best.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the extra lesson רבי ישמעאל learns from the plain words of the פסוק. It describes a case where the מזיק must give his own best land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally רבי ישמעאל only requires land as good as the ניזק's best. But if the מזיק's poor land is worse than that, it does not count, so the מזיק must pay from his good land. This is how 'his best', the מזיק's best, still means something for רבי ישמעאל.

keyTerms.meaning: Best-quality land
Worst-quality land
The one who did the damage and must pay
The one who was damaged
The best
Collect payment

steps.whatToRemember: For רבי ישמעאל, the ניזק's best land sets the standard of 'best'. If the מזיק's poor land falls below that standard, he must pay from his own best land.

phrases.english: The verse is effective:
for example, where the one who damaged has
best land and worst land,
and the damaged person has best land;
and the damager's worst land is not worth as much
as the damaged person's best land,
he pays him from his own best,
phrases.notes: 'His own' means the מזיק's own best land. That is the plain meaning of 'שדהו' that רבי ישמעאל keeps.

phrases.english: for he cannot say to him:
Come, you collect from the worst land;
rather, he collects from the best.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַהֲנִי קְרָא – כְּגוֹן דְּאִית לֵיהּ לְמַזִּיק עִידִּית וְזִיבּוּרִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the 'verse is effective' half of step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The plain פסוק teaches that when the מזיק's worst land is below the ניזק's best, the מזיק must pay from his own best land.

steps.title: What is the קל וחומר for הקדש?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to the ברייתא, quotes רבי עקיבא's line about a קל וחומר להקדש, and asks what it means.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא says: the verse comes only to let damaged people collect from the best land, and all the more so for הקדש. What is this 'all the more so for הקדש'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the ברייתא and quotes רבי עקיבא's words. This is setting up the next move: a question about which case the 'קל וחומר להקדש' refers to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא says that if regular damaged people collect from the best land, then הקדש surely does too. But the גמרא is not sure what situation he means, so it asks. The answer will come in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The verse comes only to teach
To collect payment
A logical 'all the more so' argument
Property belonging to the בית המקדש

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says:
The verse comes only
to let damaged people collect from the best land,
and all the more so for consecrated property.
What is "all the more so for consecrated property"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the רבי ישמעאל discussion and returns to the next line of רבי עקיבא's words in the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which case the קל וחומר להקדש is talking about, and how the argument works.

steps.title: The case cannot be an ox that gored a הקדש ox
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the קל וחומר is about a regular ox goring a הקדש ox. It rejects this right away, because the פסוק says 'שור רעהו', so when an ox gores a הקדש ox no damages are paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it means our ox gored an ox belonging to הקדש, that cannot be, because the Torah says 'the ox of his fellow', and not an ox of הקדש.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a first explanation of רבי עקיבא's קל וחומר להקדש and immediately knocks it down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קל וחומר about how הקדש collects for damage only makes sense if הקדש collects for damage in the first place. The פסוק 'שור רעהו' limits damage payments to an ox owned by a fellow person. That leaves out a הקדש ox, so in that case nothing is paid at all, and there is nothing to learn about which land to pay from.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say. This opens a suggestion that is about to be rejected.
Property that belongs to the בית המקדש
The ox of his fellow. These words limit damage payments to an ox owned by another person.
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean that damaging הקדש is allowed. It only means that the Torah's damage-payment laws for a goring ox don't apply when the injured ox belongs to הקדש.

phrases.english: If you say that our ox gored
phrases.notes: 'Our ox' means an ox that belongs to a regular Jewish owner.

phrases.english: an ox of הקדש,
the Merciful One said 'the ox of his fellow',
and not an ox of הקדש!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילֵּימָא דִּנְגַח תּוֹרָא דִידַן לְתוֹרָא דְהֶקְדֵּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a first answer to the question in step 26 and rejects it in the same breath.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects reading the קל וחומר להקדש as a case of damage done to a הקדש ox.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The פסוק 'שור רעהו' leaves out a הקדש ox, so there is no damage payment to measure from the best land.

steps.title: The case is a vow to give money for the upkeep of the בית המקדש
steps.stepSummary: Instead, the קל וחומר is about someone who vowed a מנה for בדק הבית. The גזבר comes and collects from his best land.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it refers to one who says, 'I take upon myself to give a מנה for the upkeep of the בית המקדש.' The treasurer comes and collects from his best land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new answer: the קל וחומר is about a person who owes money to הקדש because of a vow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is no longer about damage. It is about a debt to הקדש that came from a promise. The קל וחומר says that if a regular damaged person collects from מיטב, then הקדש should surely collect from the best land too, so the גזבר takes from עידית.

keyTerms.meaning: A sum of money equal to 100 זוז
The upkeep and repair fund of the בית המקדש
The treasurer of the בית המקדש
Best-quality land

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that רבי עקיבא's קל וחומר spreads the 'best land' rule from damage cases to debts owed to הקדש.

phrases.english: Rather, it refers to one who says
'It is upon me to give a מנה for the upkeep of the בית המקדש',
that the treasurer comes
and collects from the best land.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לָאוֹמֵר הֲרֵי עָלַי מָנֶה לְבֶדֶק הַבַּיִת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected damage case from step 27 with a vow case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which case does רבי עקיבא's קל וחומר להקדש refer to?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It refers to someone who vowed money for בדק הבית. The גזבר collects that debt from the best land.

steps.title: The treasurer should be no better than an ordinary creditor
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to challenge the new answer: why should the גזבר collect more than a regular בעל חוב?
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him be no more than a creditor,
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is starting a challenge to the vow explanation. The rest of the argument continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The vow created a regular debt, so the גזבר is really just a lender collecting a loan. The גמרא suggests he should be treated like any ordinary creditor and not get a better kind of land. The details of what a creditor collects will be spelled out next.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it be no more than. This compares one case to a weaker one.
A creditor, someone who is owed money

phrases.english: Let him be no more than a creditor,
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the גזבר. The sentence keeps going after this line.
